newsitem.title: UK: British unemployment tumbles to five-year low.
newsitem.headline: British unemployment tumbles to five-year low.

text.p: British unemployment fell to a five-and-a-half year low of just 7.2 percent in October, official figures showed on Wednesday.
An unexpectedly large 40,800 fall in the number of jobless to 2.03 million may have been exaggerated by a change in the system of benefits for the unemployed, the Office for National Statistics said.
But, as the unemployment rate hit its lowest level since February 1991, employment minister Eric Forth said jobless queues were still shrinking at a healthy rate.
"We feel this figure is somewhat overstated because of the transition to the jobseekers allowance system that we implemented just a month ago," Forth said.
"But the underlying fall is very much in line with the last few months and we're still talking about a fall of about 15-20,000 per month. We're on trend for that."
The government replaced traditional unemployment benefit with the jobseekers allowance last month. The new scheme makes more demands on claimants in terms of actively looking for work.

The ONS said job centres were struggling with backlogs of claims following the switch to the new system. That could have exaggerated October's jobless fall by about 10-15,000 and may result in a bounceback next month.

Nonetheless, economists said the unemployment figures, coupled as they were with unit wage cost growth up to 5.2 percent in the three months to September, tipped the balance in favour of interest rate rises before elections due by May 1997.

Underlying average earnings growth held steady at an annualised 4.0 percent in September, but the number of long-term unemployed -- those without work for a year or more -- is now at its lowest level since October 1991.
"These numbers will certainly maintain the Bank of England pressure for further rate rises in the months before the election," said Cooperative Bank economist Andrew Snowball.

Evidence of that pressure came in minutes from the September 13 monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, released at the same time as the jobless data.
At the meeting, George called for base rates to be raised to 6.0 percent immediately and warned that base rates might have to climb even further in the months ahead.

Clarke bit the bullet and agreed to raise rates by a quarter-point to six percent after their next monetary meeting on October 30. But the latest minutes suggest George may not be satisfied with that alone.

"The real worry for the market will be the big increase coming through in unit labour costs," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at BankAmerica. He said Clarke may be able to ward off pre-election rate rises if he produces a tight budget on November 26 -- comprising minimal tax cuts and spending cuts that at least offset any giveaways.
"But I admit in the light of today's numbers, and if we see additional strength in tomorrow's RPI, we will almost certainly have to see another quarter-point rise before polling day."

October retail price inflation figures are due on Thursday. Economists forecast the underlying rate, excluding mortgage interest payments, will jump to 3.1 percent from 2.9 in September. The government is committed to a medium-term inflation target of 2.5 percent.
Analysts said there could be another reason for the apparently massive cut in jobless numbers in October -- the government's benefits fraud hotline, set up three months ago.
The hotline has received more than 100,000 calls and a spokesman said a large proportion of them concerned people claiming unemployment benefit while working.
"The hotline appears to be succeeding in stopping people signing on," said Philip Uglow, UK economist at Union Plc.
The ONS said the number of existing claimants who did not pick up their benefit in October was 17 percent higher than a year ago.
